sections.h2: Who bills and collects property tax in Nash County?
sections.html:
Nash County combines the tax assessor and the tax collector into one office that lists, appraises and assesses real and personal property and collects the tax on it. The office is at 120 W. Washington St., Suite 2058, in Nashville, NC 27856, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the main number is 252-459-9824.

The same office takes applications for the tax relief programs that state law allows. A separate Collections page says the collector handles the money side, while questions about listing, billing and assessed values go to the assessor's side.

Each spring the Board of County Commissioners sets the rate, which must be adopted by June 30. The bill applies that rate to every $100 of taxable value. Bills are mailed in July or August, and the county asks owners who have not received one by September 15 to contact the collector.

sections.h2: How big is Nash County, and what are homes worth here?
sections.html:
Nash County has an estimated 99,365 residents as of July 1, 2025, and covers 540.44 square miles of land. The Census Bureau counted 175.7 people per square mile in 2020, and the population has grown 4.6% since the April 2020 base.

  • Median value of owner-occupied homes, 2020-2024: $191,000.
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 63.6%.
  • Median gross rent: $953.
  • Housing units, July 1, 2025: 45,068.
  • Mean travel time to work: 23.7 minutes.
  • Veterans living in the county, 2020-2024: 5,784.

With 63.6% of homes owner-occupied, a meaningful share of Nash County houses are rentals, and landlords should remember that the county bills the owner of record on January 1 even when a tenant pays the rent.

sections.h2: When are Nash County property taxes due, and what does a late payment cost?
sections.html:
Real estate and personal property tax is due September 1 and payable through January 5, the county says, and a Saturday or Sunday January 5 pushes the deadline to the next business day. A mailed payment counts as on time if it is postmarked by then, and the county urges mailing at least five business days early.

After the deadline, interest on real estate and personal property accrues at 2% for January and an additional three-fourths of one percent each month after, matching G.S. 105-360. Registered motor vehicle accounts follow a different rule, with 5% in the first month past due.

  • Unpaid real estate accounts can be advertised in local newspapers from March 1 to June 30, and the cost is added to the taxpayer's bill.
  • Collection tools include wage garnishment, bank account attachment, rent attachment, foreclosure and debt setoff against state income tax refunds.
  • The county accepts prepayments toward a coming bill, and the tax office can give details.

sections.h2: What happens to the Nash County tax bill when I sell my house?
sections.html:
The seller stays on the hook for the year's bill. The county explains that real estate tax is the legal obligation of the owner of record on January 1, and a mid-year sale does not erase the seller's liability.

Taxes are normally prorated at closing, so ask the closing attorney or your agent whether that happened. If you want to be certain nothing is left unpaid, you can have the closing paid straight to the Tax Collector's Office. If the current year's bill is not yet due, the collector will accept a prepayment based on the previous year's rate.

The lien rules back this up. A tax lien attaches to the parcel as of the listing date under G.S. 105-355, and a buyer or lender will not want to take title with that lien open. Ask the Nash County Tax Department for a payoff figure before you set a closing date.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Nash County property value?
sections.html:
You start with an informal appeal and move to the Board of Equalization and Review only if that fails. Taxpayers cannot skip a step, according to the county's revaluation page.

For the informal step, the county lists four ways to file.

  • In person, by appointment with an appraiser at the office on West Washington Street in Nashville.
  • By phone, arranging a call back from an appraiser.
  • By mail, completing the bottom of the appeal notice and sending it with supporting documents to the Tax Office, attention Board of Equalization and Review.
  • Online, through the county's informal appeal form.

The appellant has thirty days after the date on the notice to file a formal appeal with the Board of Equalization and Review, and the owner has the burden of proof. Under G.S. 105-322 the board first meets no earlier than the first Monday in April and no later than the first Monday in May.

The county's FAQ says the board looks only at the fairness and accuracy of the value, not at whether you can afford the tax, and that comparable properties with lower assessments make the best evidence. A denial can go to the Property Tax Commission within 30 days of the mailed decision (G.S. 105-290).

sections.h2: Which Nash County relief programs and deadlines apply?
sections.html:
Nash County lists four relief programs on its Tax page: the elderly and permanently disabled exclusion, the disabled veterans' exclusion, the circuit breaker deferment program and the builder's inventory exclusion. To request an application, call (252) 459-1222 or download one from the county's tax forms page.

Nash County tax filing dates (county Tax page and state statutes)

Elderly or disabled exclusion, disabled veterans, circuit breakerApply by June 1

For 2026 the Department of Revenue prints a $38,800 income limit for the elderly or disabled exclusion and circuit breaker, plus a $58,200 cap for the higher circuit breaker tier. The elderly or disabled exclusion removes the greater of $25,000 or half of the appraised value of a home (G.S. 105-277.1), while disabled veterans get the first $45,000 excluded with no age or income test.

sections.h2: How does revaluation work in Nash County?
sections.html:
North Carolina requires every county to reappraise all real property at least once every eight years, as of January 1 of the scheduled year (G.S. 105-286). Nash County's own page describes the purpose as an accurate and equitable assessment of every parcel.

The county's revaluation covers more than 53,000 parcels. It engaged an outside appraisal firm, Piner Appraisal, and informal appeals go through that firm's appraisers. Owners receive a notice of the new assessed value, and the informal clock runs from the date on that notice.

Market value, as the county defines it, is the price a willing, able buyer and seller would agree on with neither under pressure. The definition leaves out foreclosure and family sales. If your house recently sold on those terms, expect an appraiser to ask for different comparables.

faqs.q: When are Nash County property taxes due?
faqs.a: They are due September 1 and payable through January 5, or the next business day if January 5 falls on a weekend. After that, 2% interest applies for January and three-fourths of one percent per month follows.

faqs.q: Do I still owe the Nash County tax bill if I sell my house mid-year?
faqs.a: Yes, unless it is paid at closing. The county treats the owner of record on January 1 as legally responsible, and a sale does not remove that. Taxes are usually prorated, or you can have the Tax Collector paid directly at closing.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Nash County assessment?
faqs.a: Start with an informal appeal by phone, mail, online or in person with an appraiser. If that fails, file a formal appeal with the Board of Equalization and Review within thirty days after the date on the informal notice.

faqs.q: What is the deadline for Nash County tax relief applications?
faqs.a: The county asks for the elderly or disabled, disabled veteran, circuit breaker and builders' inventory applications by June 1. Classified-parcel exemptions on the AV-10 form are due January 31.

faqs.q: What is the late listing penalty in Nash County?
faqs.a: The penalty is 10%. Personal and business personal property listing forms must reach the county by January 31, and late listings are charged that penalty as the law requires.
